tagline: A little more wonder. A lot more understanding.

pages.headline: The good side of screens.
pages.deck: This month: children's code that runs in space, young inventors fixing real problems, and a paper game where you get to be the algorithm.

pages.headline: Welcome to The Guided Planet

letter.text: Hello, and welcome to our very first issue. This is a newspaper about the good side of screens: the brilliant things children make, discover and share with technology, and the clever questions worth asking along the way.

Every month we visit six places on our planet. The Discovery Observatory is for space and science, and the Maker District is for inventing. In the Thinking Forest we work out how technology really works. The Connection Garden is all about friendship, the Research Room checks what scientists actually know, and the Family Explorer is full of things to do together.
Every fact has its source printed on the same page, so you can always check where it came from. Checking is a superpower. We hope you use it.

pages.headline: The children's code travelling above Earth
pages.standfirst: Young people's code runs on the International Space Station. Last season, 25,707 of them were due to have a program run in space.[[s4]] This season, you could be one of them.

art.alt: The International Space Station on its dotted orbit above the curve of the Earth, beside a small computer whose grid of coloured lights shows a smiling pixel face.

body.text: On board the International Space Station are small computers called Astro Pis, and young people on Earth get to program them.[[s1]]

In Mission Zero, run by the European Space Agency with the Raspberry Pi Foundation, you write a short Python program that shows a picture on an Astro Pi, using its colour sensor to pick the background.[[s1]] It all happens in a web browser.[[s1]]

Young people aged 19 or under at a UK school or club can enter, alone or in a team of up to four, with a mentor such as a teacher or parent.[[s3]] Every team whose code runs gets a certificate showing where the space station was at the time.[[s1]]

facts.label: The deadline for Mission Zero entries, at 12 noon CET.[[s2]]
The ages Mission Zero is ideal for, though you can enter up to 19.[[s5]][[s3]]
Young people who took part in Mission Zero last season, 2025 to 2026.[[s4]]

activity.title: Design your space picture
activity.intro: The Sense HAT, the board made for the space station's Astro Pi computers, has a screen of 64 coloured lights in an 8 by 8 grid.[[s6]] Plan your picture here first.
steps: Pick up to four colours from the key, or choose your own.
Colour one square at a time. Each square is one light.
Keep it bold: a planet, a pet, a smiley face or your initial.
With a grown up, use the free Mission Zero guide to turn it into code. First names only, the rules say.[[s1]][[s2]]

pages.headline: Young inventors. Big ideas. A world of possibilities.
pages.standfirst: Coolest Projects is a free showcase where young people up to 18 share the things they make with technology.[[s9]] This year's favourites show what happens when you start with someone who needs help.

facts.label: young people in the online showcase[[s8]]

art.alt: An illustrated street of workshops in the Maker District, with a big gold gear and lit windows in every building.

body.text: The judges picked their favourite projects of 2026.[[s8]] Here are four of them, described the way their makers described them. We have used first names only, because that is how the showcase lists them.

projects.name: Helping Leonidas breathe better
projects.what: A home made station, built with a Raspberry Pi computer, that keeps an eye on how clean the air is indoors.[[s10]]
projects.why: Made for a real person, and his name is in the title.

projects.name: Sub Racers
projects.what: A 3D racing game made as a tribute to ocean conservation and to David Attenborough's 100th birthday.[[s11]]
projects.why: Made to help people think about the challenges facing our oceans.[[s11]]

projects.name: Ornimetrics
projects.what: A smart bird feeder that uses AI to recognise which kinds of birds come to visit, as they arrive.[[s12]]
projects.why: Technology that helps you notice nature, rather than miss it.

projects.name: HopeLink
projects.what: An app that helps people in Toronto quickly find nearby shelter, food, medical care, hygiene and transport services.[[s13]]
projects.why: Built for the people in a city who need help the most.

pages.headline: Design your own invention
pages.standfirst: Every project on page 4 began with one question: who needs help, and with what? Start with a person, not a gadget.
pages.friendSays: I've invented a robot that finds lost socks. It's brilliant. It's also missing a wheel. I know it's here somewhere.

activity.title: My invention blueprint
activity.intro: Fill in each box. Draw big, label everything, and do not worry if it would be hard to build. Every inventor starts on paper.

prompts.label: Draw it
prompts.hint: Draw your invention here. Add arrows and labels to show what each part does.

prompts.label: The problem
prompts.hint: What is the problem, and who has it? Write their name or draw them.

prompts.label: How it helps
prompts.hint: What does your invention do to make things better for them?

prompts.label: What it notices
prompts.hint: Light, sound, movement, heat, or a button being pressed?

prompts.label: What it does back
prompts.hint: Does it light up, make a sound, move, or show a message?

prompts.label: Name it
prompts.hint: Give it a name worth remembering.

prompts.label: Test it
prompts.hint: How would you know it works? Who would you ask to try it?

tips: Ask the person with the problem what they think. Good inventors listen first.
Most gadgets work the same way: something notices, a program decides, and something happens.
Stuck? Build a model from a cereal box and some tape before you draw.
Want to make it for real one day? Page 10 has free places to start.

pages.headline: Not all screen time tells the same story
pages.standfirst: Grown ups often ask how long is too long. Scientists are finding a more useful question: what are you actually doing on the screen, and who are you doing it with?[[s14]]

kinds.name: Creating
kinds.examples: Coding a game, making music, drawing a comic.
kinds.says: You are the one making the choices.

kinds.name: Learning
kinds.examples: A how to video, a maths game, a space website.
kinds.says: In one big review, watching together with a parent was linked with better reading and writing skills.[[s14]]

kinds.name: Connecting
kinds.examples: A video call with Grandma, a message to a friend.
kinds.says: Talking with people you know is different from scrolling past strangers. See page 7.

kinds.name: Watching
kinds.examples: Shows, videos, scrolling through a feed.
kinds.says: Fun, and worth noticing: did you choose it, or was it chosen for you? Page 8.

found.text: In 2024, scientists brought together 102 earlier research summaries covering almost two million young people.[[s14]] Some kinds of screen use were linked with small to moderate harms and some with benefits, so they advised weighing up each kind separately.[[s14]]
One example: screen time was linked with weaker reading and writing skills overall, but when parents watched together with their children, the link went the other way.[[s14]]

cannot.text: Most of these studies spot links, not causes: two things happening together, not one making the other happen.[[s15]] Many also rely on people estimating their own screen time.[[s15]]

Simple labels are argued about too. A review of 40 studies, mostly of adults, found little support for 'active' social media use being good and 'passive' use being bad.[[s16]] It tells us little about children your age.

askTogether: Think about yesterday. Which of the four kinds did you do most?
Which kind leaves you feeling good? Which is hard to stop?
What is one thing you would like to make, not watch, this week?
pages.friendSays: Two things happening together does not mean one caused the other. Spotting that is a skill for life.

pages.headline: Sometimes a screen helps a friendship travel further
pages.standfirst: A video call can bring a cousin from across the country into your kitchen. Scientists are learning when screens help friendships, and when they get in the way.

art.alt: Two homes on two green hills far apart, joined across the valley by a dotted gold line and a tin can telephone, with flowers growing in between.

body.text: Lots of families use video calls and messages to stay close to people who live far away, like grandparents, cousins or a friend who has moved.

In one experiment, 130 young people aged about 12 did a stressful task. The ones who then texted a friend they knew were in a better mood afterwards than the ones who sat quietly or watched a video.[[s18]] It was one short experiment, so it does not prove that more messaging is always better.

A UNICEF project that studied children aged 8 to 12 found that digital games can support feeling connected to other people, and that different games support different things depending on how they are designed.[[s20]]

pages.friendSays: A kind message can travel a very long way. Who would smile if they heard from you today?

activity.title: Send a friendship postcard
activity.intro: Cut it out, draw on the front, write on the back, then post it or hand it over.
lines: Add a stamp and an address with a grown up
Or take a photo of it and send it together

aside.label: Keep your garden safe
items: Connect with people you know in real life, and let a grown up know who.
A message from someone you do not know? Tell a grown up. You are never in trouble for telling.
Many apps, including TikTok, are for ages 13 and over.[[s21]]

pages.headline: Who chose the next video? You, or the algorithm?
pages.standfirst: When one video ends and another is already waiting, somebody chose it. Bloop went looking for clues.

art.alt: A diagram of a recommendation machine. Four signals go in at the top, labelled watched, liked, skipped and searched. A guess comes out at the bottom, labelled next up.

pages.friendSays: Case closed! The algorithm is a very fast guesser. It uses the clues you leave behind, and you are still the one holding the play button.

clues.title: An algorithm is a list of rules
clues.text: It is a list of steps for solving a problem or getting something done, a bit like a recipe, and the steps have to be in the right order.[[s23]]

clues.title: It remembers what you watch
clues.text: YouTube says the videos you have watched help it choose what to recommend to you.[[s22]]

clues.title: It notices what you search for
clues.text: What you search for changes what it suggests later on, too.[[s22]]

clues.title: You can tell it no
clues.text: Pressing 'Not interested' helps it learn what to stop suggesting.[[s22]]

body.text: So who chose? A bit of both. The algorithm makes a guess from what you did before, and you decide whether to press play.
For grown ups: a UK framework, Education for a Connected World, suggests children aged 7 to 11 learn to explain how search engines work and how their results are selected and ranked.[[s25]]

tryThis: Next time you watch with a grown up, look at the suggestions and guess why each one was picked.
Play Become the Algorithm on the next page, with paper cards.
Ask what it never shows you. Things you have not looked for yet are hiding there.

pages.headline: Become the Algorithm
pages.standfirst: One of you is the Watcher and one of you is the Algorithm. Can the Algorithm work out what the Watcher likes, using nothing but clues?
pages.friendSays: I played the Algorithm and kept showing football. My friend wanted dinosaurs. I needed more clues!

activity.title: Become the Algorithm
activity.intro: A guessing game about how recommendations work.
setup: Cut out the 12 video cards and shuffle them.
The Watcher secretly picks a favourite topic and tells nobody.
The Algorithm deals three cards face up. These are the suggestions.
rounds: The Watcher picks one card to watch, or skips all three.
The Algorithm writes down what was watched or skipped.
The Algorithm uses the clues to choose the next three cards.
After round five, the Algorithm guesses the favourite topic. Swap jobs and play again.
talk: How quickly did the Algorithm work out the favourite?
Which cards were never shown? Why not?
If the Watcher skipped everything, what could the Algorithm learn?
Real apps use clues like these, only far more of them and far faster.

tips: Older readers can try Common Sense Education's free lesson AI Algorithms: How Well Do They Know You?, made for ages 11 to 18.[[s26]]
Make your own cards with your family's favourite topics, and play again.

pages.headline: Seven days of curiosity
pages.standfirst: One small thing a day for a week. Tick a circle for everyone who joins in, then compare notes on day seven.
pages.friendSays: Thursday is my favourite. I'm still looking for the last piece of mine.

days.title: Make a pixel picture
days.task: Colour the 8 by 8 grid on page 3. Can a grown up guess what it is?

days.title: Five minutes of sky
days.task: Go outside after dark with a grown up and count the stars you can see.

days.title: Spot the guess
days.task: Watch one thing together. Talk about why the next suggestion appeared.

days.title: Fix a problem
days.task: Ask someone at home what annoys them, then design a fix on page 5.

days.title: Send a smile
days.task: Finish your friendship postcard from page 7 and send it.

days.title: Learn it together
days.task: Find a how to video, watch it together, then try it for real.

days.title: Show and tell
days.task: Everyone shows one thing they made or found out this week.

sources.quote: You will write a Python program to display a personalised image (or animation) on an Astro Pi computer on board the ISS. No special hardware or prior coding skills needed.

sources.title: Mission Zero eligibility
sources.supports: Aged 19 or younger at submission, at a school, club or registered home school in an eligible country including the UK; teams up to 4; a mentor such as a teacher or parent.

sources.org: Sanders, Noetel, Parker and colleagues, Nature Human Behaviour
sources.title: An umbrella review of the benefits and risks associated with youths' interactions with electronic screens
sources.supports: 102 meta-analyses (2,451 studies, about 1.9 million participants); small to moderate associations that depend on the type of screen use; literacy negatively associated overall but positive with parental co-viewing.
sources.quote: screen use was negatively associated with literacy (r = -0.14) but this effect was positive when parents watched with their children (r = 0.15)... carefully weigh the evidence for potential harms and benefits of specific types of screen use
sources.note: Associations, mostly from correlational studies; 95 of 102 meta-analyses at medium to high risk of bias.

sources.org: Kaye, Orben, Ellis, Hunter and Houghton, IJERPH
sources.title: The Conceptual and Methodological Mayhem of 'Screen Time'
sources.supports: Findings are mixed and lack causal evidence; measures are mostly self report.
sources.quote: Existing research presents mixed findings, and lacks longitudinal evidence for any causal or long-term effects... the use of non-standardised measures that are predominantly self-report

sources.org: Valkenburg, van Driel and Beyens, New Media and Society
sources.title: The associations of active and passive social media use with well-being: A critical scoping review
sources.supports: Across 40 studies, most did not support the hypothesised active good, passive bad associations.
sources.quote: Most studies did not support the hypothesized associations of ASMU and PSMU with well-/ill-being.
sources.note: Of the studies reviewed, most were of adults and only a minority of (pre)adolescents, so it does not speak for 7 to 12 year olds.

sources.org: Yau, Reich and Lee, Journal of Adolescent Health
sources.title: Coping With Stress Through Texting: An Experimental Study
sources.supports: 130 adolescents, mean age 12.41; texting a friend after a stressor gave higher mood than no activity or watching a video.
sources.quote: Participants who texted their friend reported higher moods... than those in the no activity condition... and higher moods than adolescents in the passive-phone condition.
sources.note: One lab session with a friend the young person already texted regularly. Mood was higher than both comparison groups; stress was lower only than the sit quietly group. Mean age 12.4.

sources.title: Responsible Innovation in Technology for Children (RITEC), phase 2 report
sources.supports: Digital games can contribute to children's wellbeing, including relationships, and different games support different aspects depending on design; samples included children aged 8 to 12.
sources.quote: digital games can indeed contribute to the well-being of children... not all games are equal: different games support different aspects of well-being depending on how they are designed.
sources.note: Co-founded with the LEGO Group and funded by the LEGO Foundation. Mixed methods, small samples.
